reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics / Pediatric Nephrology (Avner)
clinicalPearls: A ciliopathy combining juvenile nephronophthisis with an inherited retinal dystrophy, so it links the kidney and the eye through shared ciliary gene defects
The retinal component ranges from severe early-onset Leber congenital amaurosis, often with the IQCB1 or CEP290 genotype, to a milder later retinitis pigmentosa
Nephronophthisis typically presents with polyuria, polydipsia, secondary enuresis, anaemia, and growth failure before progressing to end-stage kidney disease, commonly in the second decade
Renal ultrasound shows normal or small kidneys with increased echogenicity, loss of corticomedullary differentiation, and sometimes cortico-medullary cysts
Inheritance is autosomal recessive and it overlaps genetically with isolated nephronophthisis, Joubert syndrome, and other ciliopathies
Early recognition of the eye disease in an infant with nystagmus and poor vision should prompt renal surveillance, and vice versa
Diagnosis rests on the combination of nephronophthisis and retinal dystrophy confirmed by electroretinography and molecular genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: Senior-Loken syndrome is caused by biallelic variants in nephronophthisis-associated genes that encode proteins localising to the primary cilium, basal body, and centrosome. Defective ciliary function in renal tubular epithelium leads to progressive tubulointerstitial nephropathy with tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis, and cyst formation at the corticomedullary junction, the hallmark of nephronophthisis. The same proteins are essential for the connecting cilium of photoreceptors, so their loss produces photoreceptor degeneration and inherited retinal dystrophy, explaining the combined renal and retinal phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated juvenile nephronophthisis without eye involvement
Joubert syndrome with renal and retinal features
Leber congenital amaurosis without renal disease
Other tubulointerstitial nephropathies causing polyuria in childhood
additionalInvestigations: Renal ultrasound for kidney size, echogenicity, and corticomedullary cysts
Renal function testing and urinalysis to detect concentrating defect and progression
Electroretinography and formal ophthalmological assessment for retinal dystrophy
Molecular genetic testing using a nephronophthisis or ciliopathy gene panel
Brain MRI where Joubert-related features are suspected
Assessment of growth and haematological status for chronic kidney disease complications
redFlags: Progression to end-stage kidney disease requiring dialysis or transplantation
Rapidly declining vision in an infant suggesting Leber congenital amaurosis
Growth failure and anaemia signalling advanced chronic kidney disease
Electrolyte disturbance from severe polyuria and salt wasting
reference.prognosis: The renal disease is progressive and most affected individuals reach end-stage kidney disease during childhood or adolescence, requiring renal replacement therapy. Visual prognosis depends on the retinal genotype, ranging from profound early blindness to slowly progressive visual loss.
pitfalls: Missing the renal diagnosis in a child evaluated only for visual impairment
Overlooking nephronophthisis because kidneys appear normal-sized on ultrasound
Attributing polyuria and enuresis to behavioural causes rather than a renal concentrating defect
Failing to test for the ciliopathy overlap that may include neurological features
